title: Live Video Streaming
seoTitle: Design a Live Video Streaming Platform like Twitch
description: Design a live streaming platform — ingesting broadcaster streams, real-time transcoding into an adaptive bitrate ladder, low-latency delivery through CDNs, and live chat at massive fan-out.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.text: Understanding the Problem

blocks.title: What is Live Video Streaming?
blocks.text: A live streaming platform lets a broadcaster send video from their computer or phone and lets thousands to millions of viewers watch it a few seconds later, while chatting alongside the stream. Unlike video on demand, nothing is pre-processed: every step has to happen in real time.
Functional Requirements
Core Requirements

items: Broadcasters should be able to start a live stream.
Viewers should be able to watch a live stream with only a few seconds of delay.
Viewers should be able to send and see chat messages for a stream.
Streams should be recorded and available for replay after they end.

blocks.text: Below the line (out of scope):

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

blocks.text: Non-Functional Requirements
Core Requirements

items: Glass-to-glass latency of about 2-5 seconds for normal streams.
Smooth playback across varied networks — adapt quality instead of buffering.
Scale to ~100k concurrent streams and individual streams with millions of viewers.
Highly available: a single server failure must not end a broadcast.

blocks.text: Below the line (out of scope):

items: Strong consistency for chat ordering across all viewers.

blocks.text: The Set Up
Defining the Core Entities

items: **Channel**: a broadcaster's identity and their secret stream key.
**Stream**: one live broadcast session — status, start time, ingest server, renditions.
**Segment**: a short chunk (1-2 s) of encoded video at one quality level.
**Chat message**: user, stream, text and timestamp.

blocks.text: API or System Interface

blocks.code:
RTMP/SRT  rtmp://ingest.example.com/live/{streamKey}     (broadcaster push)
GET  /streams/:streamId/master.m3u8                      -> playlist of renditions
GET  /streams/:streamId/{rendition}/playlist.m3u8        -> latest segments
GET  /streams/:streamId/{rendition}/{segment}.m4s        -> video chunk (via CDN)
WS   /streams/:streamId/chat                             -> send / receive messages
GET  /streams/:streamId/replay                           -> VOD playlist

blocks.text: High-Level Design
1) Broadcasters can start a live stream

Broadcasting software (OBS, a mobile app) pushes video over **RTMP or SRT** to the nearest **ingest server**, using the channel's stream key. The ingest server authenticates the key with the **Stream Service**, marks the stream live, and forwards the raw feed to transcoding.
2) Viewers can watch with a few seconds of delay

The transcoder encodes the feed into an **adaptive bitrate ladder** (e.g. 1080p, 720p, 480p, 160p) and cuts each rendition into **1-2 second segments** (HLS or DASH with CMAF). Segments and updated playlists are written to an **origin**, and viewers fetch them through a **CDN**. The player picks the rendition matching its bandwidth and switches between them as conditions change.
3) Viewers can chat

Viewers open a **WebSocket** to a chat server. A message is published to the stream's chat channel (Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka topic), and every chat server with viewers of that stream fans it out to its connected clients. Messages are also persisted for moderation and replay.
4) Streams are available for replay

Because segments already exist at every quality, a replay is just a **VOD playlist** listing the stream's segments in order. Segments are copied from the origin to durable object storage (S3) as they're produced, so the recording is ready the moment the stream ends.
Potential Deep Dives
1) How do we keep latency down to a few seconds?

approach.text: Use 6-10 second segments and let players buffer three segments before playing.

challenges.text: Latency becomes 20-30 seconds — chat reactions arrive long before viewers see the moment they're reacting to.

approach.text: Cut segments to 1-2 seconds with a keyframe at each boundary, and have players start near the live edge with a smaller buffer.

challenges.text: Latency drops to ~6-10 seconds, but every segment still has to be fully encoded, uploaded and fetched before playback, and many tiny files increase request overhead.

approach.text: Use **Low-Latency HLS** (or LL-DASH): each segment is split into **partial chunks** of ~200-500 ms that are published as soon as they're encoded, and the CDN streams them using chunked transfer while the rest of the segment is still being produced. Playlists support **blocking reloads**, so players learn about new parts immediately instead of polling. Players hold a ~2-3 second buffer and speed up playback slightly when they drift behind.

challenges.text: Requires CDN support for chunked transfer and blocking requests, and smaller buffers mean less tolerance for network hiccups — offer a "low-latency" toggle per stream.

blocks.text: 2) How do we serve millions of viewers on one stream?
Every viewer requests the same few segments at the same moment, which is a perfect fit for caching — as long as the origin isn't hit once per viewer.

approach.text: Players request segments directly from the origin servers.

challenges.text: A million viewers each fetching a 1 MB segment every 2 seconds is ~4 Tbps from the origin — impossible.

blocks.title: CDN in front of the origin

approach.text: Serve segments through a CDN with short TTLs on playlists and long TTLs on segments (segments never change once written).

challenges.text: When a new segment appears, thousands of edges miss at the same instant and stampede the origin.

approach.text: Put a **mid-tier shield** layer between edges and the origin, and enable **request collapsing**: concurrent misses for the same segment wait on a single upstream fetch. The origin sees roughly one request per shield per segment, regardless of audience size. Very popular streams can be **pushed** proactively to edges.

challenges.text: Shields must be sized for peak events, and multiple CDNs may be needed for the largest broadcasts.

blocks.text: 3) How do we transcode 100k concurrent streams?

Real-time transcoding is the biggest cost. A fleet of transcoder workers (GPU or hardware encoders) is scheduled by a **job scheduler** that assigns each new stream to a worker with capacity, near its ingest PoP. To control cost, only popular or partner streams get the full ladder; small streams may get **source-quality passthrough** plus one lower rendition, and are upgraded automatically when viewers grow. If a transcoder dies, the scheduler reassigns the stream and the player rides through on its buffer.
Mention the cost trade-off explicitly: most streams have very few viewers, so transcoding everything into five renditions wastes most of the compute.
4) How does chat scale for a stream with a million viewers?

A million viewers typing produce more messages than anyone can read. Rate-limit senders, and on huge streams **sample** or batch messages per chat server (deliver at most N per second, with priority for moderators and subscribers). Fan-out uses a two-level hierarchy: the stream's channel delivers to chat servers, and each server delivers to its local connections, so a message is published once and copied only at the edge.
Final Design

quiz.question: Why are live streams split into short segments?
options: So players can download and switch quality chunk by chunk via ordinary HTTP and CDNs
quiz.explanation: Segments make live video cacheable HTTP objects and enable adaptive bitrate switching.

quiz.question: What mainly drives latency in standard HLS?
options: Segment duration multiplied by the number of buffered segments
quiz.explanation: Players buffer several full segments before playing, so long segments mean long delay.

quiz.question: How do we stop thousands of CDN edges stampeding the origin when a new segment appears?
options: A shield tier with request collapsing
quiz.explanation: Collapsing concurrent misses into one upstream fetch keeps origin load independent of audience size.

quiz.question: Why not transcode every stream into a full bitrate ladder?
options: Most streams have few viewers, so the compute cost is mostly wasted
quiz.explanation: Full ladders are reserved for popular streams; others get fewer renditions until their audience grows.
